solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Like this clue, a burden?

parts.note: the load in 'a heavy one to bear'

explanation.surface: A solver sighs that this particular clue is a real burden to work out.
explanation.walkthrough: A CROSS to bear is a burden. The definition points at the clue itself: it is 1 Across, and the question mark flags that self-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-referential definition: this clue sits in the across list, so it is literally an across clue.

clue.text: Right to enter a Cricket Club eagerly seeking success primarily

indicators.note: primarily means 'first of all', so take the first letter of each word

explanation.surface: A cricket club hungry for success gets the right to enter a competition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right to enter' reads as the start of a sentence about the club, but it is the definition, and the wordplay simply strings A, CC and three initials together.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: having access to a building means having the right to go in.

clue.text: Strangely goes ape — a first significant life event

indicators.note: the letters behave strangely, turning up in a new order

parts.note: all thirteen letters of GOES APE A FIRST, rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone goes wild for the first time at a big moment in their life.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash invites you to read 'goes ape' as the whole story; it is simply the start of the thirteen letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A rite of passage is a ceremony or milestone marking a move to a new stage of life, such as coming of age.

clue.text: Footballer, one refusing to work

definitions.meaning: an attacking player whose job is scoring goals

explanation.surface: A footballer downs tools and won't play.
explanation.walkthrough: Read together, the two halves suggest a lazy player; the comma actually separates two unrelated meanings of one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the forward who strikes the ball, and the employee on strike.

clue.text: Internet image, satnav, a target partly

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the answer sits inside them

parts.note: runs from the last two letters of satnav, through 'a', into the start of target

explanation.surface: A list of gadget words: an online picture, a satnav, something to aim at.
explanation.walkthrough: Ignore the comma: satn-AV A TAR-get holds the answer across three words.
explanation.definitionFit: An avatar is the picture or figure that stands for a user online, a specific kind of internet image.

clue.text: Six take examination — look in

explanation.surface: Six pupils sit an exam while someone pops in to check.
explanation.walkthrough: Crosswords often turn numbers into Roman numerals; 'Six' here is VI, not a count of students.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to look in on someone is to make a short visit.

clue.text: Pretend not to notice extremely untidy dinner table, sadly

indicators.note: the letters are in a sorry state and must be rearranged
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A host ignores a dinner table left in a mess after the meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the ends of 'untidy' join the letters of DINNER TABLE before the whole lot is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom, supposedly from Nelson putting his telescope to his blind eye to ignore a signal.

clue.text: Forest worker's team from Glasgow cutting back

indicators.note: cut the back end off the word, losing its last letter

parts.note: one of Glasgow's two big football clubs, the rival of Celtic

explanation.surface: A forester's favourite football team is Glasgow's, trimming its costs.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's is short for 'is', linking definition to wordplay rather than showing possession.
explanation.definitionFit: A forest ranger is employed to patrol and look after woodland, so a worker in the forest.

clue.text: One providing food in new career (enthralling time)

indicators.note: a new version of the word has its letters in a fresh order
to enthral is to hold captive, so the rearranged letters hold the next piece

parts.note: standard abbreviation, held after the second letter

explanation.surface: Someone starting a new career in food finds it takes up all their time.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'enthralling time' look like an aside about the job, but they hold the container step: T goes inside the shuffled CAREER.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a caterer's business is supplying food and drink for functions.

clue.text: One telling tales near court is out of order

indicators.note: the letters are out of their proper order and must be rearranged

parts.note: the nine letters of NEAR COURT rearranged

explanation.surface: A telltale hanging round a courtroom is behaving improperly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telling tales' suggests a sneak, but here it just means a storyteller.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a raconteur is someone admired for telling anecdotes well.

clue.text: Wrong about sappers captivating woman

indicators.note: one word goes around the other

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, placed before the last letter of SIN

explanation.surface: It is wrong for army engineers to fall for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappers are military engineers; in crosswords they are the RE, the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: A siren is an alluring, dangerously attractive woman, after the singers of Greek myth who lured sailors.

clue.text: Frighten spy

definitions.meaning: the verb: to scare or startle
the noun: informal for a secret agent

explanation.surface: An order to scare a secret agent.
explanation.walkthrough: Two words, two definitions: one verb, one noun, the same answer for both.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the verb for scaring someone and the slang noun for an intelligence agent.

clue.text: Modest accommodation with somewhere to sleep at start of tourist period

indicators.note: the letter at the start of a word is its first, so keep only that one

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A modest holiday let with a bed, just right for the start of the tourist season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tourist period' reads as the holiday season; split it, and each word does its own job.
explanation.definitionFit: A cottage is a small, simple country house, so modest accommodation.

clue.text: Endless school lesson, private, recalled by a learner

indicators.note: called back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: inner thoughts are private; turned round to RENNI
the L on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: An interminable school lesson, remembered by a pupil in private.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Private' looks like a soldier (PTE) but here means INNER; only that word turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Perennial means lasting indefinitely or constantly recurring, so near enough endless.

clue.text: The setter's favourite American drive?

parts.note: a pet project is a favourite one

explanation.surface: The setter asks about their favourite road trip in the States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' looks like a journey by car in the surface; it is the noun for motivation.
explanation.definitionFit: Impetus is the force or drive that makes something happen.

clue.text: Part of exotic act using New World plant

indicators.note: only part of the words is used, so the answer sits inside them

parts.note: runs from the last letter of exotic, through act, into the start of using

explanation.surface: A circus performer's exotic act features a plant from the Americas.
explanation.walkthrough: exoti-C ACT US-ing holds the answer; 'New World' is the Americas, where cacti come from.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by origin: cacti are native to the Americas, the New World.

clue.text: Friend coming up to power computer

indicators.note: in a down clue, coming up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a pal is a friend; turned round to LAP

explanation.surface: A friend comes over to switch on the computer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming up to' reads as 'approaching'; split it, since 'coming up' reverses PAL and 'to' is kept as letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a laptop is one kind of computer, a portable one.

clue.text: Pacify beast, initially unkindly caged, shunning outsiders

indicators.note: initially means 'at the beginning', so only the word's opening letter is used
leave out the outside letters, keeping the middle

explanation.surface: Advice on calming an animal that has been cruelly locked up and kept apart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caged' looks like a container instruction, but it is only the word whose middle is kept.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used of feelings: to assuage anger or fear is to calm it down.

clue.text: Following drink, right lively?

indicators.note: the second piece follows the first

explanation.surface: After a drink, is one really livelier?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right' reads as 'really' in the surface; in the wordplay it is the abbreviation RT, placed after the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Alert means quick-witted and wide awake, a sense of lively.

clue.text: Photographed at first with a large animal

indicators.note: at first means 'at the beginning', so only the word's opening letter is used

explanation.surface: A tourist has their picture taken alongside a big animal at the zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word, but it supplies AND.
explanation.definitionFit: The giant panda is a large bear-like animal.

clue.text: Business I omitted from rant

indicators.note: the letter is left out of the word

parts.note: the I is taken out of TIRADE

explanation.surface: A businessperson's speech has had the self-centred 'I' cut out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads backwards to its instruction: find the word for rant first, then remove the I.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: trade and business both mean buying and selling commercially.

clue.text: Note delightful surprise — go back

parts.note: the second note of the scale, do-re-mi
a treat is a delightful surprise

explanation.surface: A message says there's a lovely surprise waiting, so head back home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' looks like a written message; it is the musical note RE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from warfare: an army that retreats withdraws to where it came from.

clue.text: Roughly hustle investigator

indicators.note: the letters are handled roughly, knocked into a new order

parts.note: the six letters of hustle rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone pushes a detective about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly hustle' reads as manhandling; 'Roughly' is the instruction to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, slightly old-fashioned: a sleuth is a detective, from the sleuth-hound that tracks by scent.

clue.text: Out, like Prime Minister once after retiring

indicators.note: the second piece comes after the first
retiring means drawing back, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel, 19th-century British Prime Minister; turned round to LEEP

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister in retirement is out of the picture.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Peel was British Prime Minister in the 1830s and 1840s. 'Retiring' also nods to going to bed, which fits being out cold.
explanation.definitionFit: Out, as in 'out like a light', means asleep.
